entities.summary:
The Battle of the Granicus was a pivotal clash between Macedonian forces under Alexander the Great and the Persian satraps in 334 BCE. This battle marked the beginning of Alexander's conquest of the Persian Empire, which would ultimately stretch from Greece to India. The Granicus River, in modern-day Turkey, was the site of this decisive battle.

The Battle of the Granicus was a turning point in world history, as it led to the fall of the Persian Empire and the rise of the Hellenistic period. Alexander's victory allowed him to expand his empire, which would have far-reaching consequences, including the spread of Greek culture and language across the ancient world. The battle also showcased Alexander's military tactics and leadership skills, which would become legendary in history.

The Battle of the Granicus is remembered as a triumph of the Macedonian phalanx formation, which proved to be a decisive factor in the battle. Alexander's forces, led by Parmenion and Hephaestion, employed the phalanx formation to devastating effect, breaking through the Persian lines and securing a crushing victory.

In the years that followed, Alexander's empire would continue to expand, eventually encompassing a vast territory that stretched from Greece to Egypt, Babylon, and Persepolis. The legacy of the Battle of the Granicus can be seen in the spread of Greek culture, language, and philosophy throughout the ancient world, which had a profound impact on the development of Western civilization.
